WCAG 2.2 adds nine new success criteria to the rules of web accessibility, six of which count towards level AA conformance, and removes one. They are becoming the basis of the European standard EN 301 549 V4.1.1, of the forthcoming RGAA 5 in France and of the next Luxembourg frameworks. For each of the WCAG 2.2 new success criteria, this guide sets out what it really requires, the failure we come across most often, the fix in HTML or CSS, and the test your team can run itself in a few minutes.

WCAG 2.2 at a glance: nine new success criteria, one removed

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023; the current version was updated on 12 December 2024. WCAG 2.2 builds on WCAG 2.1 without replacing it: every existing rule is kept, with one exception, and nine success criteria are added. The official page What’s new in WCAG 2.2 presents them with examples of the users they help.

These criteria mainly address needs that earlier versions covered poorly: people who navigate with a keyboard and lose sight of the active element, people with tremors or reduced fine motor control, and people with cognitive, memory or learning disabilities. They affect components found on almost every website: sticky headers, consent banners, icon buttons, sliders, checkout flows and login forms.

The nine success criteria added in WCAG 2.2
CriterionLevelWhat it requires, in one sentenceComponents most affected

2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)AAANo part of the focused element is hidden.Same components
2.4.13 Focus AppearanceAAAThe focus indicator has a minimum area and contrast.Focus styles in the design system
2.5.7 Dragging MovementsAAAnything done by dragging can also be done with a single click or tap.Sliders, drag and drop, kanban-style boards, maps
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)AAClickable targets measure at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with exceptions.Icons, pagination, close buttons, date pickers

Success criterion 4.1.1 Parsing is declared obsolete and removed. In total, WCAG 2.2 contains 86 active success criteria. Level AA conformance, the level targeted by every European regulation, requires the level A and AA criteria: among the new ones, that means 2.4.11, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.2.6, 3.3.7 and 3.3.8. The three AAA criteria remain good practice that you can aim for on sensitive user journeys, with no regulatory obligation.

To place WCAG within the wider set of frameworks (EN 301 549, RGAA, RAWeb, eCH-0059), our article WCAG 2.2, EN 301 549, RGAA, RAWeb: which digital accessibility standard to follow gives the overall picture. This article goes down to component level, criterion by criterion. And if you are new to the subject, start with our guide to digital accessibility, which sets out the obligations and the users concerned.

When the WCAG 2.2 new success criteria become mandatory in your country

WCAG is not a law: it becomes mandatory when a legal text or a national framework refers to it. Yet most of the frameworks in force in November 2026 are still based on WCAG 2.1. The move to WCAG 2.2 is therefore happening country by country, at the pace of new versions of the standards. This time lag explains a common situation: a website declared compliant in one country may fail several WCAG 2.2 criteria without currently being in breach of the law.

Framework in force and move to WCAG 2.2, by country (November 2026)
Country or frameworkFramework in forceWCAG basisMove to WCAG 2.2

Belgium, public sectorEN 301 549 V3.2.1 standardWCAG 2.1When V4.1.1 is cited in the Official Journal of the EU
Luxembourg, public sectorRAWeb 1.1 and RAAM 1.1EN 301 549 V3.2.1, hence WCAG 2.1RAWeb 2 and RAAM 2, announced for February 2027
Switzerland, ConfederationeCH-0059 version 3.0WCAG 2.1No revision timetable known to date
European Union, European Accessibility ActRequirements of Directive (EU) 2019/882EN 301 549 standard as a means of demonstrating conformityEN 301 549 V4.1.1, published in September 2026, citation in the OJEU expected

In France, the official RGAA 5 announcement by DINUM, the French government’s digital directorate, states that the new version will incorporate WCAG 2.2 and that its criteria will clarify or supplement those of RGAA 4.1.2 without contradicting them. At European level, the EN 301 549 V4.1.1 standard was published by ETSI on 2 September 2026; its chapters on the web, documents and software are aligned with WCAG 2.2. In Luxembourg, the SIP (Service information et presse) has announced the move of RAWeb and RAAM to version 2, in line with this standard.

Key takeaway

Fixing the six new level A and AA criteria now costs less than dealing with them after RGAA 5 or RAWeb 2 is released: most of them are resolved in a handful of shared components, and audits carried out against EN 301 549 V4.1.1 already check them.

For a business subject to the European Accessibility Act, the question arises differently. The directive sets requirements in terms of outcomes; the harmonised standard is the simplest way of demonstrating that you meet them. As soon as V4.1.1 is cited in the Official Journal, it, and therefore WCAG 2.2, will be the reference used by market surveillance authorities. Our article on what the authorities check under the European Accessibility Act describes these checks sector by sector.

2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured: the active element must not disappear under a banner

The wording of the criterion is short: when a user interface component receives keyboard focus, it is not entirely hidden by author-created content. A person navigating with the Tab key, a screen magnifier or voice control needs to be able to see where they are. If the active link slips under a sticky header, they are typing blind.

The typical failure

Three situations account for most failures. The first is the sticky header: when moving back up the page with Shift+Tab, the browser scrolls just far enough to bring the link to the top of the window, where the header covers it. The second is the cookie consent banner fixed to the bottom of the screen, which hides the footer for the whole visit until it is closed. The third is the floating chat or back-to-top button, which covers a field or button located in the same corner.

The criterion does not forbid fixed elements; it forbids them from entirely hiding the active element. The W3C documentation, Understanding 2.4.11, adds two useful nuances. Content opened by the user themselves, such as a drop-down menu they have just expanded, may cover the active element. And if the user can reveal the element without moving focus, for example by closing a non-modal panel with the Escape key, the element is not considered obscured.

The fix

For a sticky header, the simplest fix is a single line of CSS on the root element: scroll-padding-top with a value equal to the height of the header, for example “html { scroll-padding-top: 5rem; }”. Recent browsers then reserve that space when they scroll the page to bring an element into view; check this with the keyboard in the browsers your audience uses. The same logic applies at the bottom of the page with scroll-padding-bottom, if an action bar stays fixed at the bottom on mobile.

For the cookie banner, two options are safe: place it in the page flow, at the top, rather than as a fixed overlay; or make it modal, that is, move focus inside it and keep it there until the user makes a choice. The worst option is a fixed, non-modal banner that can neither be reached easily with the keyboard nor ignored. For a floating button, reserve a margin at the bottom of the page so that no interactive content ends up underneath it.

The test you can run yourself

  1. Smaller window set the browser to a width of 1,280 pixels and then to a mobile format, with 200% zoom, where fixed elements take up the most space.
  2. Full tab-through go through the whole page with Tab, then back up with Shift+Tab, without closing the cookie banner on the first pass.
  3. Observation at each stop, check that at least part of the active element remains visible; note any elements that are completely hidden and the component covering them.
  4. Second pass repeat the run with the banner closed, then on secondary templates: article, product page, form, search results.

At level AAA, criterion 2.4.12 goes further: no part of the element may be hidden. And criterion 2.4.13 Focus Appearance requires the focus indicator to cover at least the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter around the component, with a contrast of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states. Neither criterion is mandatory, but a focus style designed to meet 2.4.13 settles once and for all the debates about focus visibility (criterion 2.4.7, level AA, criterion 10.7 of RGAA).

2.5.7 Dragging Movements: an alternative to drag and drop

The criterion requires that any functionality that uses a dragging movement can be achieved with a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the functionality is determined by the browser and not modified by the author. A dragging movement means pressing down, moving the pointer while keeping the button or finger down, then releasing. This gesture is difficult, or even impossible, for a person with tremors, someone using a head or eye-gaze pointing device, or voice control.

It should not be confused with criterion 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures, which has existed since WCAG 2.1 and covers gestures that follow a path or use several fingers. Criterion 2.5.7 covers simple dragging, where only the start point and end point matter. Nor is it about the keyboard: a component can be perfectly usable with a keyboard and still fail 2.5.7, because a person using a mouse or a touchscreen does not necessarily have a keyboard.

Typical failures

  • a custom price or volume slider that can only be adjusted by dragging the handle;
  • a list to reorder (priorities, steps, favourites) by drag and drop only;
  • a kanban-style tracking board where you change the status of a card by dragging it from one column to another;
  • a file drop zone with no “Browse” button;
  • an interactive map that can only be moved by dragging it, with no panning buttons;
  • a before/after comparison slider whose divider only moves when you pull it.

The fix

The fix consists of adding a simple click path that coexists with dragging. For a slider, a click on the track should move the handle to that point, and “minus” and “plus” buttons or a number field should allow the value to be entered. The native “input type=range” control is often the best starting point: its behaviour is partly handled by the browser. For a list to reorder, add “Move up” and “Move down” buttons to each item, or a “Move to…” menu. For a kanban board, a status menu on each card is enough.

Another pattern works well: select the item with a click, then click on the destination. This is the behaviour users expect from file management interfaces, and it never requires holding a button down. For the drop zone, the “Browse” button that opens the operating system’s file picker is the standard solution. For a map, panning and zoom buttons, or an address search field, meet the need.

The test

The test is mechanical: for each component that responds to dragging, try to achieve the same result using simple clicks only, without ever holding the mouse button down. On mobile, do the same with simple taps. If a function can only be performed by dragging, and dragging is not essential (a handwritten signature or freehand drawing, for example), the criterion fails.

2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum): 24 CSS pixels and five exceptions

Criterion 2.5.8 requires the size of the target for pointer inputs to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. A CSS pixel is the unit used in the style sheet, not the physical pixel of the screen: on a high-density phone, 24 CSS pixels correspond to many more physical pixels. The rule is aimed at people with tremors or reduced fine motor control, but also at anyone using a phone with one hand.

The criterion provides for five exceptions, which you need to know so as not to fix things unnecessarily:

  • Spacing: a smaller target is acceptable if a circle 24 CSS pixels in diameter, centred on its bounding box, does not intersect another target or the circle of another undersized target;
  • Equivalent: the same function is available through another control on the page that meets the size requirement;
  • Inline: the target is in a sentence, like a link in a paragraph, or its size is constrained by the line height of the text;
  • User agent control: the size is determined by the browser and not modified by the author, like an unstyled native checkbox;
  • Essential: a particular presentation is essential or legally required, like the pins on a map that must stay at their geographical position.

The Understanding 2.5.8 documentation illustrates the circle method: you draw a 24 CSS pixel circle centred on each small target and check that no circle overlaps a neighbouring target or another circle. In practice, a 16-pixel icon can pass if it is sufficiently isolated, whereas a row of 20-pixel icons placed side by side fails.

Typical failures

Failures are concentrated in a few patterns: tightly packed numeric pagination (“1 2 3 … 12”); the close button of a modal window or banner, often drawn at 12 or 16 pixels; share or action icons lined up with no margin; the days of a date picker on mobile; carousel navigation dots; clickable star ratings; and the “+” and “−” quantity buttons in a shopping basket. In a purchase journey, those last two cases come up constantly; our screen-by-screen e-commerce accessibility checklist places them in the context of the checkout flow.

The fix

The size that counts is that of the clickable area, not the drawing. A 16-pixel icon can stay visually identical if its button is given padding that brings the clickable area up to 24 pixels: for example “.icon-button { min-width: 24px; min-height: 24px; }” with the icon centred. For a row of tightly packed links, increase the spacing with the “gap” property of a flex or grid container. Make these fixes in the design system: a single, correctly sized icon button component resolves hundreds of occurrences.

Level AAA retains criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), which requires 44 by 44 CSS pixels. That is a good target for the main buttons of a mobile app or a kiosk. Teams that have already adopted the sizes recommended by the iOS and Android design guidelines generally meet 2.5.8 with no extra effort.

The test

  1. Identify small targets in the browser’s developer tools, inspect icons, isolated links and custom form controls; note their computed width and height.
  2. Apply the exceptions for each target smaller than 24 pixels, check the spacing (circle method), whether an equivalent control exists or whether the target is “inline”.
  3. Check on mobile repeat the inventory on a mobile template, where icons are often smaller and closer together.

3.2.6 Consistent Help: the help link in the same place on every page

Criterion 3.2.6 does not require you to offer help. It requires that, if a web page contains a help mechanism and that mechanism is repeated on several pages within a set, it appears in the same order relative to other content, unless the user initiates a change. The absence of help on some pages is not in itself a failure: the criterion only applies to pages that offer it. Four mechanisms are covered: human contact details (phone number, email address, opening hours), a human contact mechanism (contact form, live chat with an adviser), a self-help option (FAQ, help page) and a fully automated contact mechanism (chatbot).

The rule protects people with cognitive or memory disabilities, for whom finding help is already an ordeal. If the “Contact” link is in the header on the home page, in the footer on product pages and somewhere else again in the customer account area, they have to look for it again every time they change page.

Typical failures

  • the customer service phone number displayed at the top of editorial pages but at the bottom of account pages;
  • a chat assistant placed in different positions depending on the template;
  • a checkout flow or online application process, built by another supplier, which reuses the site’s common elements but places the help link in a different order;
  • an FAQ linked from the main menu on the website and from the footer in the customer account area.

The fix and the test

The fix is a matter of governance more than code: decide once and for all where the help mechanisms are located (for example, a “Help and contact” link in the same position in the header of every template) and require that location of the teams and suppliers who build separate journeys. The test consists of opening the main templates side by side and checking that each help mechanism present appears in the same relative order. It is quick, but it often fails on websites built by several teams.

3.3.7 Redundant Entry: don’t ask users again for what they have already given

Under criterion 3.3.7, information previously entered by or provided to the user that is required to be entered again in the same process is either auto-populated or available for the user to select. There are three exceptions: re-entering the information is essential, it is required to ensure the security of the content, or the previously entered information is no longer valid.

The word “process” matters: the criterion covers a series of steps to complete a task, such as an order, an application for social benefits or a registration. It does not require information to be remembered from one visit to the next. Nor should it be confused with criterion 1.3.5 (level AA, criterion 11.13 of RGAA), which requires the purpose of personal data fields to be identified with the autocomplete attribute; the two complement each other.

Typical failures

  • the billing address requested again just after the delivery address has been entered, with no “same as delivery address” checkbox;
  • a multi-step form that asks again for the name or case number entered at the first step;
  • a summary page that forces the user to retype a field in order to correct it, instead of returning to the step with the value preserved;
  • going back in the checkout flow clears fields that had already been filled in.

The fix

The solutions are well known: a checkbox that copies the delivery address into the billing address; fields pre-filled with the values entered at earlier steps; a drop-down list of addresses already entered in the process; and values kept when the user goes back. The security exceptions still apply: asking for a new password twice to confirm it does not cause the criterion to fail.

To test, go through each multi-step journey noting every piece of information entered, then check at each new step that none of it is required again without pre-filling or a choice. Also test the journey’s own “Back” button and the browser’s. This test naturally belongs in the accessibility acceptance testing of every new version of a form.

3.3.8 Accessible Authentication: passwords, codes and CAPTCHAs

This is the criterion with the greatest consequences for customer accounts, banks, insurers and online public services. It forbids requiring a cognitive function test at any step of an authentication process, unless that step provides an alternative or a mechanism to assist the user, or the test consists of recognising objects or personal content supplied by the user. A cognitive function test, as defined by WCAG, is a task that requires the user to remember, manipulate or transcribe information: for example remembering a password, copying characters, doing a calculation or solving a puzzle.

Passwords are therefore not forbidden. The Understanding 3.3.8 documentation cites two valid forms of assistance: support for password managers, which remove the need to remember, and copy and paste, which removes the need to transcribe. A password field that works with autofill and accepts pasting meets the criterion. It is blocking these aids that causes it to fail.

Typical failures

  • a password field that blocks pasting (an “onpaste” handler that returns false);
  • a login form whose fields are not recognised by password managers (username and password on two separate pages without the autocomplete attribute, dynamically generated fields with no name);
  • a virtual keypad whose digits change position at each login, with no other method;
  • a code received by SMS or email that has to be typed into six separate boxes which refuse pasting;
  • a CAPTCHA that asks the user to copy distorted text, with no other way of logging in;
  • a request for specific characters of the password (“enter the 2nd, 5th and 7th character”), which prevents autofill.

The fix

In the code, the autocomplete attributes do most of the work: “autocomplete=username” on the username field, “autocomplete=current-password” on the login password, “autocomplete=new-password” when the account is created and “autocomplete=one-time-code” on the one-time code field. The first three allow password managers to fill in the fields; the last one allows many mobile browsers to suggest the code received by SMS. For the code, prefer a single field to six separate boxes; if the design requires boxes, pasting a complete code into the first box must fill in the others.

Login methods that do not rely on any cognitive test are valid alternatives: a login link sent by email, passkeys based on biometrics or the device’s unlock code, or login via an authenticator app that only asks for a simple confirmation. Strong authentication is not the issue: a second factor meets the criterion as long as the code can be pasted or filled in automatically, or a method without a code is offered.

For CAPTCHAs, level AA tolerates object recognition (“select all images containing a bicycle”) and identification of content supplied by the user, such as an image they chose when registering. Level AAA, with criterion 3.3.9, removes these two exceptions. A CAPTCHA based on transcribing distorted text fails in all cases if no alternative exists. Bear in mind that a visual CAPTCHA also causes problems for blind people under other criteria, notably 1.1.1 on text alternatives.

The test

  1. Password manager save a test account in the browser’s password manager and check that it fills in the username and password on the login screen.
  2. Pasting copy the password and the one-time code, then paste them into their fields; pasting must work, including into separate boxes.
  3. Other steps review every step: account creation, forgotten password, second factor, re-authentication before a sensitive operation.
  4. CAPTCHAs identify each CAPTCHA and check its type and whether an alternative exists.

Criterion 4.1.1 removed: what it changes for an audit

Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing required HTML code free of structural errors: opening and closing tags, unique IDs, no duplicated attributes. The W3C declared it obsolete because assistive technologies no longer parse HTML code themselves: they rely on the parsing done by browsers, which now handle errors reliably; the real problems it targeted are covered by other criteria, such as 1.3.1 Info and Relationships or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value.

The practical consequence depends on the framework. An audit against WCAG 2.2 or EN 301 549 V4.1.1 no longer tests this criterion. For WCAG 2.0 and 2.1, the W3C has added a note stating that this criterion should be considered always satisfied for HTML or XML content. But a national framework may keep its own check: that is the case in France for as long as RGAA 4.1.2 applies, with its criterion 8.2 on source code validity. EN 301 549 V3.2.1, applied in Belgium and on which RAWeb 1.1 is based in Luxembourg, also still contains the corresponding requirement. So do not remove code validation from your acceptance testing procedures until your national framework has changed.

WCAG 2.2 new success criteria and national frameworks: how to audit in 2026

None of the nine new criteria has a direct equivalent in RGAA 4.1.2, which is based on WCAG 2.1. A website can therefore show an RGAA compliance rate of 100% and still fail 2.5.8, 3.3.7 or 3.3.8. This situation is normal today, but it has two consequences. First, the rate shown in the accessibility statement says nothing about conformance with WCAG 2.2. Second, the next update of the statement, carried out against RGAA 5, is likely to lower the rate if nothing has been fixed.

Two audit approaches are possible during the transition. The first is to carry out the official audit against the framework in force, for the statement, and add a check of the six new A and AA criteria, presented separately in the report. The second is to audit directly against WCAG 2.2 or EN 301 549 V4.1.1, which suits businesses subject to the European Accessibility Act and organisations operating in several countries. Our article on how an RGAA audit unfolds, week by week shows where this additional check fits in, and an EN 301 549 conformance audit covers all the WCAG 2.2 criteria.

Which audit for which organisation during the transition
SituationFramework for the official auditWCAG 2.2 check to add
French public bodyRGAA 4.1.2 (statement)The six new A and AA criteria, in a separate section
Luxembourg public bodyRAWeb 1.1 or RAAM 1.1The six new criteria, in preparation for RAWeb 2 and RAAM 2
Belgian public bodyEN 301 549 V3.2.1The six new criteria, in preparation for V4.1.1
Business subject to the EAAEN 301 549 V4.1.1 (WCAG 2.2 AA)Already included

For statements, stay consistent: the accessibility statement names the framework actually used and must not mix compliance rates. The most common errors, together with an annotated template, are presented in our article on the errors that make an accessibility statement invalid. In Luxembourg, where the move to RAWeb 2 is announced for February 2027, the page digital accessibility in Luxembourg summarises the obligations of public bodies.

Mobile apps and documents: the new criteria apply too

WCAG was written for the web, but EN 301 549 applies its criteria to software, including mobile apps, and to documents. The WCAG 2.2 text remains the reference; the W3C also publishes interpretation notes explaining how to apply each criterion outside the browser: WCAG2ICT for non-web technologies and, still at the draft note stage, WCAG2Mobile for mobile apps. In an app, the new criteria that fail most often are target size (toolbar icons, close buttons), authentication (a code field that does not suggest the code received by SMS) and dragging movements (reorderable lists, swipe actions with no equivalent menu).

For an iOS or Android app, testing is done on a real device, with VoiceOver or TalkBack, and with switch control or voice control for dragging. In Luxembourg, RAAM is the framework for public sector apps; elsewhere, the audit follows EN 301 549. A mobile app audit against RAAM checks these points on both platforms. For PDF documents, the new criteria have little effect: they mainly target interactions that documents do not include, with the exception of fillable PDF forms.

WCAG 2.2 upgrade plan: where to start

The good news is that the new criteria are rarely fixed page by page. They are fixed in a few shared components and in design rules. The table below ranks the six A and AA criteria by where the fix is made and the usual scale of the work; the actual scale depends on your architecture and on the share of third-party components.

Where to fix each new A and AA criterion
CriterionWhere the fix is madeUsual scaleWho is involved
2.4.11 Focus Not ObscuredGlobal style sheet, consent banner, fixed elementsLowFront-end integration
2.5.8 Target SizeDesign system components: icon button, pagination, date pickerLow to mediumDesign and front-end
3.2.6 Consistent HelpHeader and footer templates, third-party journeysLowProduct, editorial governance
3.3.7 Redundant EntryLogic of multi-step formsMediumFront-end and back-end development
2.5.7 Dragging MovementsInteractive components: sliders, lists, kanban boards, mapsMedium to highDevelopment, design
3.3.8 Accessible AuthenticationLogin screens, second factor, CAPTCHAs, identity providerVariable: low if you control the code, high if a third-party service is involvedDevelopment, security, procurement

Start with the quick, high-impact fixes (obscured focus, target size, consistent help), which can often be resolved in a single iteration. Then tackle authentication, because it blocks access to everything else in the service: a person who cannot log in cannot do anything else. Leave complex drag-and-drop components until last, as they sometimes require the interaction to be redesigned. If the login screen or the CAPTCHA is provided by a supplier, the fix goes through the contract: require conformance with WCAG 2.2 AA in your next procurements.

The WCAG 2.2 checklist to give your teams

  • the page scrolls so that the active element never passes entirely under the sticky header (scroll-padding-top set);
  • the cookie banner is in the page flow or modal, never fixed and non-modal on top of the content;
  • no floating button covers interactive content;
  • every icon button, close button and pagination number offers a clickable area of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or meets the spacing exception;
  • every slider can be adjusted by clicking on the track, with buttons or with an input field;
  • every reorderable list offers buttons or a menu for moving items;
  • every file drop zone has a “Browse” button;
  • help and contact links, and any chat assistant, are in the same relative place on every template where they appear, including the checkout flow;
  • no information already given in a journey is requested again without pre-filling or a choice;
  • going back in a form keeps the values entered;
  • username and password fields carry the right autocomplete attributes and accept pasting;
  • the one-time code can be pasted and carries autocomplete=one-time-code;
  • no transcription CAPTCHA is imposed without an alternative;
  • source code validation stays in acceptance testing for as long as the national framework is based on WCAG 2.1.

To make these rules stick over time, build them into the definition of done for each component and into the acceptance criteria for deliveries. Our digital accessibility training courses for designers and developers cover these new criteria with code examples, and our support for accessible development lets you fix the design system together with your teams.

Six misconceptions about WCAG 2.2

Several misunderstandings keep coming up in discussions with project teams. Clearing them up avoids unnecessary fixes or, conversely, costly omissions.

  1. “Buttons need to be 44 pixels everywhere.” No: level AA requires 24 CSS pixels, with five exceptions; 44 pixels falls under criterion 2.5.5, which is level AAA.
  2. “Sticky headers are forbidden.” No: they simply must not entirely hide the active element. A single line of CSS is often enough.
  3. “Passwords are forbidden.” No: they are allowed if password managers and copy and paste work.
  4. “All CAPTCHAs are forbidden.” No: at level AA, object recognition is tolerated; it is transcription without an alternative that fails. Other criteria still apply to the CAPTCHA.
  5. “If it works with a keyboard, drag and drop is compliant.” No: criterion 2.5.7 is aimed at pointer users; a single-click method is required.
  6. “Our 100% RGAA score proves WCAG 2.2 conformance.” No: RGAA 4.1.2 contains none of the nine new criteria.

To estimate the work on your website, an audit focused on the new criteria, or adding them to a full audit, remains the most reliable approach; the factors that make the cost of such an engagement vary are detailed in our article on the price of an accessibility audit. For a French public body, the page dedicated to the public sector presents the full support we provide, from audit to accessibility statement.

Frequently asked questions

Is WCAG 2.2 mandatory in France?

Not directly yet. RGAA 4.1.2, the framework in force for public bodies and large companies, is based on WCAG 2.1. RGAA 5, announced by DINUM for the end of 2026, will incorporate WCAG 2.2. For businesses subject to the European Accessibility Act, EN 301 549 V4.1.1, which is aligned with WCAG 2.2, will become the reference as soon as it is cited in the Official Journal of the European Union.

How many success criteria are there in WCAG 2.2?

WCAG 2.2 has 86 active success criteria: the 78 criteria of WCAG 2.1, minus criterion 4.1.1 Parsing, which has been removed, plus the nine new ones. Of the new criteria, two are level A, four are level AA and three are level AAA. Level AA conformance, which European regulations require, covers the A and AA criteria.

Is a website that conforms to WCAG 2.1 also conformant with WCAG 2.2?

Not necessarily. It meets all the rules common to both versions, but it may fail the six new A and AA criteria: obscured focus, dragging, target size, consistent help, redundant entry and authentication. Conversely, a website that conforms to WCAG 2.2 also conforms to WCAG 2.1: for criterion 4.1.1, the W3C states that it is always satisfied by HTML content, but a national framework such as RGAA 4.1.2 may keep its own code validity check.

What is the minimum button size under WCAG 2.2?

Criterion 2.5.8, at level AA, requires a clickable area of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. A smaller target is still acceptable if it is sufficiently spaced from its neighbours, if another conforming control offers the same function, if it is a link within a sentence, if its size is set by the browser or if its presentation is essential. The 44 CSS pixel size corresponds to criterion 2.5.5, at level AAA.

Are CAPTCHAs banned by WCAG 2.2?

No. Criterion 3.3.8 forbids requiring a cognitive test to log in without an alternative or assistance. A CAPTCHA that asks the user to copy distorted text fails if there is no other way of logging in. An object recognition CAPTCHA is tolerated at level AA, but not at level AAA. Other criteria, such as text alternatives, continue to apply.

Do we need a new accessibility audit to move to WCAG 2.2?

Not necessarily a full audit. If your last audit is recent, a targeted check of the six new A and AA criteria on your sample of pages is often enough to plan the fixes. A full audit is justified after a redesign, when the national framework changes (RGAA 5, RAWeb 2) or when you need to produce a new accessibility statement.
